Chapter 1: The Birth of the Transistor
1947. Before silicon, there was germanium. Goal: build a transistor radio!
Ashes to Elements
Smelt coal into coal ash. Some coal deposits contain trace germanium.
Reduction
Reduce GeO2 with charcoal into metallic germanium. Still full of impurities - not nearly pure enough for a transistor!
Zone Refining
Refine germanium. A molten zone sweeps impurities to one end of the bar (Pfann, 1952).
The First Transistor
Two gold contacts pressed onto n-type germanium by a plastic wedge: the point-contact transistor (Bardeen and Brattain, 1947).
Music from Coal
Build a transistor radio. In 1954 this changed how the world listened.
Needle in a Haystack
Combine 8 coal ash into germanium concentrate. Only a tiny fraction is germanium.
Brimstone Chemistry
Burn sulfur powder in a furnace to get SO2, then dissolve it in water. Real plants oxidize SO2 to SO3 first (contact process).
Leaching
Dissolve the concentrate in acid to get germanium dioxide (GeO2).
Doping
Add a trace of phosphorus to make n-type germanium. Purify first, then add exactly the impurity you want.
The Sandwich
Indium on both sides of n-type germanium, then heat: a p-n-p alloy-junction transistor (1952).
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p1:
SEMICONDUCTOR LAB
Chapter 1: The Birth of the Transistor (1947)

Goal: build a transistor radio.

Everything here follows real chemistry. Where the game simplifies, this book says so.

Press L to see your next step.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p2:
1. GERMANIUM
Before silicon, there was germanium. It hides in two places: zinc ore (sphalerite, deep underground) and the ash of some coal.

Smelt coal for ash. Mine sphalerite with an iron pickaxe and roast it in a reverberatory furnace: every 4th gives germanium concentrate.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p3:
2. SULFURIC ACID
Burn sulfur powder (from sulfur caves) in a furnace: S + O2 -> SO2. Dissolve in water.

Simplified: real plants first oxidize SO2 to SO3 with a catalyst.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p4:
3. EXTRACT + REDUCE
Acid pulls germanium out of the concentrate as GeO2. Charcoal takes the oxygen away: metallic germanium, but still dirty.

Simplified: industry uses hydrogen, and chlorine distillation.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p5:
4. ZONE REFINING (Pfann, 1952)
Melt a narrow zone and move it along the bar. Impurities prefer the liquid, so they ride to the end.

Each pass: unrefined -> 6N -> 9N -> 10N. 9N = one impurity per billion atoms. 10N needs a synthetic graphite boat.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p6:
THE FURNACE
Graphite boat, quartz tube, copper induction coil, screw + motor.

HF oscillator (3 kW of electricity): 2 vacuum tubes + coil + Leyden jar. It ran on vacuum tubes!

Boat: clay-graphite = 9N max, synthetic graphite = 10N.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p7:
5. DOPING
Pure is not enough. Add ONE chosen impurity to the molten zone (zone leveling):
 phosphorus -> n-type (extra electrons)
 indium -> p-type (missing electrons)

Mixing solids would do nothing. Needs 9N or better.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p8:
6. TRANSISTORS
1947 point-contact: two gold contacts pressed onto n-type Ge by a plastic wedge.
1952 alloy-junction: indium on both sides of n-type Ge, then heat -> p-n-p sandwich.

A small base current controls a large current. That is the whole trick.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p9:
NO CLEAN ROOM?
Correct - in 1947 there were none. Laminar-flow clean rooms arrived in the 1960s, when one speck could kill a whole integrated circuit.

The surface of your germanium is dirty right now. Real labs etch it with acid before use.

guide2.semiconductor-lab.p1.title: Why Electricity?
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p1:
SEMICONDUCTOR LAB
Volume 2: Electricity (1830s-1900s)

Chapter 1 had two 'fakes': the furnace's power supply and its boat. Both need electricity.

Here you build a power grid, then use it to make what fire alone cannot.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p2.title: 1. Water Wheel
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p2:
1. WATER WHEEL
Put it next to FLOWING water: 500 W per side. Still water does nothing.

Power = flow x height of the fall. Many early power stations were hydro (Niagara, 1895).
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p3.title: 2. Steam
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p3:
2. STEAM
Coal boils water, steam pushes a piston, a dynamo turns: 50 kW.

One coal = 30 MJ of heat but only 1.5 MJ of electricity (5%). Watt's engines wasted most heat. The steam turbine reaches 30%.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p4.title: 3. Self-Excited Dynamo
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p4:
3. DYNAMO
Varley, Siemens and Wheatstone, 1866-67: no permanent magnet. Leftover magnetism in the iron core starts a small current, which makes the electromagnet stronger, and so on.

Right-click a water wheel or steam engine with it: 2x output.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p5.title: 4. Cables
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p5:
4. CABLES
Connected cables form one network. Cables store nothing: power goes straight from generators to machines.

Loss = 1% per cable on the longest path (P = I^2 R). Max 1 MW per network. Batteries take the surplus.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p6.title: 5. Electrolysis
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p6:
5. ELECTROLYSIS
Electricity splits water: 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2 (2:1 by volume). Sulfuric acid only carries the current.

Hydrogen reduces metals without carbon: tungsten, and the purest germanium.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p7.title: 6. Vacuum Tubes
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p7:
6. VACUUM TUBES
Pump the air out (hand pump, then a Sprengel mercury pump to 0.1 Pa), seal a hot tungsten filament, a grid and a plate in glass.

De Forest, 1906: a small grid voltage controls a big current. Two tubes make the HF oscillator for the zone refiner.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p8.title: 7. Electric Furnace
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p8:
7. ELECTRIC FURNACE
Current through graphite rods makes heat (Joule heat) up to ~1500 C, with no smoke from fuel.

Add a hydrogen tube: the hydrogen furnace.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p9.title: 8. Synthetic Graphite
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p9:
8. GRAPHITE
Acheson, 1896: pass current straight through packed coal + sand. Above 2500 C the carbon rearranges into graphite and impurities boil away.

Needs 500 kW: a steam turbine. Result: the 10N boat.
guide2.semiconductor-lab.p10.title: 9. Chlorine
book.semiconductor-lab.ch2.p10:
9. CHLORINE
Electrolyze salt water: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> Cl2 + H2 + 2NaOH. Burn H2 in Cl2: hydrochloric acid.

GeO2 + HCl -> GeCl4 (boils at 83 C). Distill it, and only then can germanium reach 10N.
zukan.semiconductor-lab.root.title: Encyclopedia
zukan.semiconductor-lab.root.description: Every item you pick up unlocks its entry here: the adult (3) and deep-dive (4) notes in full.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p1.title: Why silicon?
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p1:
Semiconductor Lab
Vol. 3: Silicon (1950s)

Germanium is rare and dislikes heat. Silicon comes from ordinary rock (quartzite) and stands heat.

This volume turns rock into 11N silicon and then a solar cell.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p2.title: 1. Quartzite
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p2:
1. QUARTZITE
Quartz veins are everywhere (about 12% of the crust is SiO2). Mine with a stone pickaxe.

No nether quartz: it does not exist in reality.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p3.title: 2. Arc furnace
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p3:
2. ARC FURNACE
SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO (about 2000 C). Quartzite 2 + charcoal 1 + 12 kWh (500 kW) -> metallurgical silicon 98%.

Silicon holds oxygen very tightly, so it takes arc heat.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p4.title: 3. Trichlorosilane
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p4:
3. TRICHLOROSILANE
Si + 3HCl -> SiHCl3 + H2 (about 300 C). Dry HCl gas, not the acid.

SiHCl3 boils at 32 C. Each distillation stage adds one 9; 9 stages give 11N.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p5.title: 4. Siemens process
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p5:
4. SIEMENS PROCESS
SiHCl3 + H2 -> Si + 3HCl on a thin rod at about 1100 C. The rod grows.

500 kW x 648 s = 90 kWh/kg. The HCl goes back. Purity = the TCS purity, 9N-11N.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p6.title: 5. Czochralski
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p6:
5. CZ
Melt at 1420 C in a single-use quartz crucible, pull a turning seed under argon.

B2O3 -> p-type, phosphorus -> n-type. Boron spreads evenly (k 0.8), phosphorus piles up (k 0.35). Oxygen comes from the quartz.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p7.title: 6. Slices
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p7:
6. SLICES
A diamond disc cuts the crystal into thin plates: 1 ingot -> 8.

The blade width turns into powder. In 1954 Bell Labs cut long strips.
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p8.title: 7. Diffusion
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p8:
7. DIFFUSION
At about 1000 C dopant soaks in from the surface. n-type slice + boron -> thin p-type top.

The boundary is the p-n junction, the heart of transistors too (Fuller 1954).
guide3.semiconductor-lab.p9.title: 8. Solar cell
book.semiconductor-lab.ch3.p9:
8. SOLAR CELL
8 p-n slices + copper cable. 60 W under the day sky (1000 W/m2 x 6%), about 20% in rain.

Bell Labs, 25 April 1954. Powered a satellite in 1958. Chapter 2 goal!

guide4.semiconductor-lab.p1.title: Why ICs?
book.semiconductor-lab.ch4.p1:
Semiconductor Lab
Vol. 4: ICs (1958-1961)

Wire transistors one by one and the joints fail as their number grows.

This volume makes the parts inside one wafer and wires them on top.
guide4.semiconductor-lab.p2.title: 1. Drafting table
book.semiconductor-lab.ch4.p2:
Draw each layer on the grid: island, base, emitter, contact, metal.

The preview and the cross-section show the result first. The scissors cut one artwork per layer.
guide4.semiconductor-lab.p3.title: 2. Photomask
book.semiconductor-lab.ch4.p3:
The reduction camera shrinks the big artwork onto a photographic plate: a photomask.

Real makers also cut big red film (Rubylith) by hand and shrank it by photography.
guide4.semiconductor-lab.p4.title: 3. Oxide
book.semiconductor-lab.ch4.p4:
The oxidation furnace grows a SiO2 film on the wafer.

This film shields the places that must not be doped.
guide4.semiconductor-lab.p5.title: 4. Resist and exposure
book.semiconductor-lab.ch4.p5:
The spin coater spreads a light-sensitive film (resist). Early ICs used negative KPR; positive resist spread in the 1970s.

The mask aligner prints the mask's shadow. Contact is sharp but wears the mask.
guide4.semiconductor-lab.p6.title: 5. Develop and etch
book.semiconductor-lab.ch4.p6:
The developer bench dissolves the exposed resist.

Hydrofluoric acid in the etch tank opens windows in the bare oxide. The stripper removes the rest of the resist.
guide4.semiconductor-lab.p7.title: 6. Planar
book.semiconductor-lab.ch4.p7:
The diffusion furnace dopes only through the windows, three times (island, base, emitter).

The junction edges hide under the oxide. This is Hoerni's planar process of 1959.
guide4.semiconductor-lab.p8.title: 7. Aluminium wiring
book.semiconductor-lab.ch4.p8:
The vacuum evaporator coats the wafer with aluminium; phosphoric acid etches it into lines.

The parts are joined by wiring on the chip: Noyce's idea of 1959.
guide4.semiconductor-lab.p9.title: 8. Probe station
book.semiconductor-lab.ch4.p9:
Set the pads to 0 V or 5 V and press Probe.

Resistor, diode, transistor, integrated circuit, NOT: a name appears only after you make it.
guide4.semiconductor-lab.p10.title: 9. Dirt
book.semiconductor-lab.ch4.p10:
Every step leaves a little dirt. A dirty chip leaks and works only sometimes.

The cleaning bench brings it back to zero.

guide5.semiconductor-lab.p1.title: Why logic?
book.semiconductor-lab.ch5.p1:
Semiconductor Lab
Vol. 5: Logic (1961-1971)

A transistor is an electric switch. Wire switches together and they can 'think'.

This volume solves challenges up to adding and remembering.
guide5.semiconductor-lab.p2.title: 1. Challenges
book.semiconductor-lab.ch5.p2:
Pick a challenge with ▶ at the probe station. It only tells you the behaviour: how to build it is up to you.

Solving one opens the next.
guide5.semiconductor-lab.p3.title: 2. Pad roles
book.semiconductor-lab.ch5.p3:
Click pads to set 0 V, 5 V, inputs A-D, clock and outputs 1-4.

Probe tries every input combination and compares the outputs.
guide5.semiconductor-lab.p4.title: 3. Near misses and hints
book.semiconductor-lab.ch5.p4:
When it fails, one line of clues appears in chat (never the answer).

? opens hints one step at a time. Solve without them for 'found on your own'.
guide5.semiconductor-lab.p5.title: 4. Stamps
book.semiconductor-lab.ch5.p5:
Solving a challenge turns the chip's shape into a stamp.

Put it in the drafting table's stamp slot and left-click to press. It never runs out.
guide5.semiconductor-lab.p6.title: 5. Symbols
book.semiconductor-lab.ch5.p6:
▣ shows pressed stamps as symbols. Click one to look inside.

Under every symbol are real mask shapes, and the probe judges the shapes.
guide5.semiconductor-lab.p7.title: 6. Everything from NOR
book.semiconductor-lab.ch5.p7:
One kind of gate, NOR (or NAND), can build any logic circuit.

Micrologic (1961) and the Apollo computer were built from NORs.
guide5.semiconductor-lab.p8.title: 7. Adding
book.semiconductor-lab.ch5.p8:
Half adder = XOR (sum) + AND (carry). A full adder also adds the carry from below.

Chain four for a 4-bit adder.
guide5.semiconductor-lab.p9.title: 8. Memory
book.semiconductor-lab.ch5.p9:
Feed outputs back into each other and the circuit remembers a bit (flip-flop, 1918).

These challenges are checked step by step: each step remembers the last.
guide5.semiconductor-lab.p10.title: 9. Counters and registers
book.semiconductor-lab.ch5.p10:
Rows of flip-flops count (counters) and store numbers (registers).

With adders and registers, the road opens to calculators and the CPU (1971).

A circuit you found became a stamp. Press it on the drafting table to build bigger circuits.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p1.title: Why smaller?
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p1:
Semiconductor Lab
Vol. 6: Shrinking (1970s-2000s)

Thinner lines put more transistors on the same chip: faster and cheaper.

This volume covers light, power, new steps and MOS.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p2.title: 1. Wavelength
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p2:
Mercury g-line 436 nm -> i-line 365 nm -> KrF laser 248 nm -> ArF 193 nm.

Shorter light prints thinner lines, deep into the ultraviolet.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p3.title: 2. Rayleigh's rule
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p3:
Line width CD = k1 x wavelength / NA.

NA is how wide an angle the lens gathers. k1 is cleverness (0.25 is the limit).

In the game the CD sets how fine the grid is.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p4.title: 3. Steppers and immersion
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p4:
A stepper prints one chip at a time through a reducing lens, then steps (1978).

Fill the gap between lens and wafer with water and NA passes 1 (immersion, 2000s).
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p5.title: 4. Moore's law
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p5:
Gordon Moore, 1965: transistors per chip double every year (two years, from 1975).

Not a law of nature but a target for fabs and lens makers.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p6.title: 5. AC and transformers
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p6:
AC flips direction back and forth. A transformer's turns ratio changes the voltage.

Send it at high voltage and the wires waste much less heat.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p7.title: 6. Rectifiers
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p7:
Many machines run on DC. A rectifier turns AC into one-way flow.

Once mercury-arc rectifiers, now semiconductor diodes.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p8.title: 7. Ion implantation
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p8:
Ionise the dopant, accelerate it and fire it in (1970s): exact dose and depth.

The crystal is damaged until an anneal heals it.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p9.title: 8. Sputtering and dry etching
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p9:
Sputtering knocks metal atoms onto the wafer and coats steps well.

Dry etching cuts straight down with plasma. Wet etching spreads sideways, so fine lines need dry.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p10.title: 9. MOSFET
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p10:
Gate voltage opens a channel under a thin oxide (Atalla and Kahng, 1960). No current flows into the gate.

Press P on the drafting table to switch to the MOS process.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p11.title: 10. CMOS
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p11:
Pair p- and n-channel MOSFETs and almost no current flows while idle (1963).

Compare the supply pad current at the probe station. That's why calculator batteries last.
guide6.semiconductor-lab.p12.title: 11. Metal 2 and CMP
book.semiconductor-lab.ch6.p12:
One wiring layer runs out. Add an interlayer oxide (CVD), a second metal and vias to join them.

Stacking makes the surface bumpy, so polish it flat (CMP).
